query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of tin (~5 at.%) to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxidation resistance at high temperature by promoting formation of a more adherent, protective oxide scale without significantly altering its room- or high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C whose oxygen resistance is inadequate.
generation.intervention: Doping the alloy with approximately 5 at.% Sn (i.e., modifying the composition to include Sn as an alloying addition).
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours under conditions similar to previous oxidation-protection studies; mechanical performance tested both at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (~1000 °C) at comparable strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a Sn-enriched, protective oxide layer at the surface that adheres well to the underlying BCC matrix and inhibits further oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: Tin segregates to the alloy’s surface during high-temperature exposure to form tin oxide, which improves the scale adhesion and acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, thereby reducing the oxidation (pesting) typically seen in untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Sn-doped alloy will exhibit significantly reduced oxide growth and pesting compared to the untreated alloy, while retaining its useful room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which shows inadequate oxygen resistance under air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours.
generation.boundary: The oxidation improvement is predicted to be effective specifically under air exposure at 800 °C for up to 5 hours, while mechanical performance is expected to be preserved in unmodified test environments used previously.
generation.uncertainty: The exact level of Sn doping that balances oxidation protection without adversely affecting the mechanical properties is not yet fully established, and there may be unforeseen microstructural changes due to Sn addition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr (control) and one set doped with ~5 at.% Sn. Subject both sets to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours. Characterize the oxidation scale (e.g., via SEM, EDS, and XPS) and subsequently perform mechanical tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C to assess ductility and yield strength.
measurements: Oxidation scale thickness and continuity (via microscopy and surface analysis)
Post-exposure tensile properties (ductility and yield strength)
Phase analysis to confirm retention of the single BCC phase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale growth or pesting (i.e., mass gain and scale integrity comparable to untreated samples) OR if its room and high-temperature mechanical properties deteriorate relative to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,].
